<section aria-labelledby="abstract"><h2 id="abstract">Abstract</h2>
<p class="paper-abstract">The global energy transition is driven by the urgent need to achieve deep decarbonization while maintaining system reliability and economic viability. Yet, the variability of renewable resources and the limited flexibility of conventional baseload power remain key barriers to large-scale integration. Hydrogen has emerged as a versatile solution, capable of providing long-duration storage, enabling sector coupling, and enhancing the operational flexibility of energy systems. This dissertation develops three distinct techno-economic analysis (TEA) frameworks that integrate optimization modeling with lifecycle financial evaluation to systematically assess hydrogen’s role in advancing sustainable energy systems. The study explores three interconnected applications. It first examines the integration of hydrogen storage with renewable generation, showing how co-location strategies reduce curtailment and improve cost-effectiveness under diverse market and resource conditions. It then broadens the scope to the grid level, using the Texas power system as a case study to evaluate how hydrogen can mitigate uncertainty in renewable deployment and demand growth, while inter-regional hydrogen networks alleviate geographic mismatches and contribute to significant carbon reductions. Building on these insights, the framework is applied to nuclear power systems, where hydrogen production enhances operational flexibility, supports participation in ancillary service markets, and creates new revenue streams—outcomes that are further reinforced under favorable policy incentives. These analyses illustrate hydrogen’s capacity to serve as a unifying energy carrier across renewable and nuclear contexts. The findings emphasize that the effectiveness of hydrogen-enabled systems depends not only on technological performance but also on evolving cost trajectories, market mechanisms, and policy frameworks. By establishing a coherent analytical foundation and offering actionable insights, this dissertation provides guidance for policymakers, industry leaders, and researchers in designing resilient, economically viable, and carbon-neutral energy pathways where hydrogen plays a central role.</p>
<p class="paper-source">Abstract source: <a href="https://henryutd2021.github.io/files/papers/li2025dissertation.pdf">PDF pages 6–7 (vi–vii)</a>.</p></section>
